I try to avoid hiking the popular trails during the summer weekends due to the crowds, so I researched a lesser known route to the top of the top of Marion Mountain (elevation 10,362) for last weekend's hike.

**Stats **

Peak: Marion Mountain, 10,362 feet (#14 on the Sierra Club's Hundred Peaks List)

Distance: 10.32 miles

Elevation gain: 4,542 feet

Time: 7 hours, 7 minutes (yikes!)

Route: Seven Pines trail to PCT to cross country route to the peak

Marion Mountain is sub-peak to Mt. San Jacinto east of Los Angeles. There is no trail to the top so you have to do some off trail cross country hiking to a Class 3/4 summit.

I passed several of the popular trail heads in the Idyllwild area that looked like the 405 at rush hour before arriving at the Seven Pines Trailhead. This trail isn't well maintained and you have to drive several miles down a winding dirt road to reach it.

Seven Pines Trailhead

Despite the trail having many fallen trees over it, it is a hidden gem.

https://i.sli.mg/t6sadT.jpg https://i.sli.mg/esoS32.jpg https://i.sli.mg/3XUirc.jpg

That's where I'm headed. Marion Mountain is on the left and the unofficially named Mt. St. Ellen's is on the right (more on that in a bit)

https://i.sli.mg/9J8kXu.jpg

Lots of cool looking rock formations on this trail.

https://i.sli.mg/Glrcxk.jpg

Into the wilderness we go.

https://i.sli.mg/PMGrqg.jpg https://i.sli.mg/Qx4oiR.jpg https://i.sli.mg/CRg47v.jpg

After briefly join up with the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), I left the trail and headed straight up the side of the mountain for nearly two miles. This steep, boulder-filled gully led all the way to the top. It was slow going and murder on the legs. I was planning on about 5 hours for this hike, but it end up taking me 7 hours due to the slow accent.

https://i.sli.mg/t1GWhd.jpg https://i.sli.mg/Z33u5v.jpg

I hit the top of St. Ellen's first. This peak was named by a local hiking club for one of their members. In the peak register, there was a small photo album. This old lady was a bad ass. She was doing some serious mountaineering into her 70s.

https://i.sli.mg/1NQuBZ.jpg https://i.sli.mg/etueUR.jpg https://i.sli.mg/qvUwSy.jpg https://i.sli.mg/gZTaCL.jpg

Looking across at the Marion summit block. I got a climb on my hands.

https://i.sli.mg/kAsOSY.jpg https://i.sli.mg/MOPJbh.jpg

After circling around, I finally found a possible way to the top.

https://i.sli.mg/fnXXuP.jpg https://i.sli.mg/8js6TC.jpg https://i.sli.mg/0pQqhc.jpg

I carefully shimmied up the crack to the top and was treated to some awesome views of San Jacinto Peak.

https://i.sli.mg/znZ3fD.jpg

I could see thunderclouds starting to form in the area and knew I needed to get off the peak soon.

https://i.sli.mg/jZYaz3.jpg

It got really dark and the thunder starting to roll, but I got back to my car about 10 minutes before the downpour started.

https://i.sli.mg/yF5jnh.jpg

Bonus Question: What's your favorite WWII movie?

Edit: i totally forgot to add mine last night, but it seems Voaters have good taste ; )

My favorite war movies are both set in Vietnam: Apocolypse Now and FMJ. Established directors, great acting, flawless scripts, and great non-combat storylines. Master and Commander is also very rewatchable and well done, but I think the previous two are still ahead.

My favorite WWII movie is Where Eagles Dare, followed by Bridge On the River Kwai, Patton, and A Bridge Too Far (in no order). The two bridge movies don't end in clear victory or defeat, and I respect movies that are good at prohibiting closure.

Double bonus round: Favorite WWI movie is Lawrence of Arabia.

Wild cards: Braveheart, Last of the Mohicans, No Man's Land

Decision before dawn.

Followed by "The Dawn Patrol."

War is hell!

For the bonus: The Big Red One.

Followed by: The Young Lions.

Both are fictional but perfectly capture the terrible flavor of war...

My favorite world war 3 film is playing out now in the 2016 presidential election.
Probably Apocalypse Now. Charlie don't surf! The jungle, god damn fucking right.

The opening scene of Saving Private Ryan was astonishing. I remember seeing it when I was around 18 and thought a good old war film would be awesome, who doesn't at that age.

Walked away from that, especially the landings, absolutely stunned. It in no way glorified war. Amazing.

The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly is a Civil War movie in my mind, so it wins.

Bonus: Probably Fist of Legend. Or Battle of Britain. Or Casablanca. It would be Band of Brothers if we let it count.
